Book of Indian Life Crafts 
Oscar E. Norbeck - - $5.95 

Here is the “how to do” for crafts 
and skills that were daily essential in 
the lives of the Indians . . . explained 
in clear text and more than 60 full- 
page pictures so that youngsters and 
oldster, beginner or veteran craftsman 
can start work immediately on any of 
the nearly 200 projects. 

Arranged for greatest appeal and 
convenience, projects deal first with 
personal items like Indian vests, moc¬ 
casins, dresses and ornaments, then 
lead to the construction of family and 
tribal artifacts such as a tepee, an 
authentic Indian garden, musical 
instruments, sports and hunting equip¬ 
ment, dance masks and other cere¬ 
monial equipment, pictographs, peace 
pipes, travois and scores more. Indian 
ceremonial, smoke signal and cooking 
fires are explained in detail, with 
proper safety precautions in their use. 

Order from your regular bookseller 

G. R. WELCH CO. LTD. 

1149 King Street West Toronto 3 


continued, from page 68 

lighting. Smith carried, or had tied to 
his saddle, a short club and when the 
battle was on he usually waded in, 
trying to hit the beast without striking 
a dog. As he was an expert with the 
club, from long practice through killing 
many coyotes over the years, he nearly 
always succeeded, though at times the 
fight might last several minutes before 
he was able to give the animal its coup 
de grace. 

This country had been originally 
buffalo land and then cattle country. 
The coyote and cows were compatible. 
In the sheep lands the coyote is a 
menace that the sheepherder must battle 
at all times. There is a fundamental 
clash between the prairie wolf and the 
man, for these animals slaughter the 
sheep whenever they are left unpro¬ 
tected. In this country the wolves were 
plentiful, they could be heard far and 
near every night, and running them 
with dogs was a popular sport. They 
occasionally raided the poultry houses, 
but not often enough to make them a 
nuisance to the farmers, for one or two 
hounds running loose in the farmyard 
would make them stand away. Running 
them with the dogs controlled and kept 
their numbers low. 

Coyotes, as they affect cattle in a 
stock country, are carrion eaters; they 
clean up the dead cows so that disease 
is controlled. Rabbits and rodents of 
other kinds are their main diet, but it 
should be stressed that this wolf will 
take the most readily available food. It 
can be rabbits, gophers, carrion livestock 
or poultry, anything is edible if they can 
get it down. They seem to prefer live 
food, for if the big jacks, or the gophers 
are plentiful the wolves will take these 
in preference to other foods. 

Bounties on these wolves were popular 
at that time. Control of animals by 
bounty has always been approved by the 
legislatures for they can be easily applied, 


92 


Canadian Camping 





give good results in skins or skulls, and 
make the minimum bother as well as 
pleasing the majority of the voters. 
Unfortunately, bounties will not control 
pests. Bounties are paid on animals that 
might be called surplus. Over the years 
the numbers of any animal will fluctuate 
widely, high in summer and becoming 
low just before the breeding season. 
When a long period is studied it is seen 
that the numbers will vary widely over 
a short period but remain almost con¬ 
stant over a long time. That is fifty 
years ago there was nearly the same 
number and provided there are no 
radical changes, such as a country grow¬ 
ing up to trees where it was formerly 
grass, fifty years from now the numbers 
will be the same as they were fifty years 
ago. Bounties, as has been shown time 
and again, will not control any creature.

UNLESS THERE IS A LIGHT 

Children fear their shadows, 

Yet have no cause for fright; 

There cannot be a shadow 
Unless there is a light. 

If you can see your shadow, 

The sight can only mean 
That light is shining, but yourself 
Has gotten in between. 

There is no less of radiance, 

But you have blocked the sight . . . 
Stop looking at the shadow, 

Start looking at the light. 

—Anon.
